text: CHAPTER 2  THEORETICAL BACKGROUND

This chapter presents the components, training methods, and evaluation measures used in CNN-based road damage classification. The discussion considers single-label multiclass classification: each image is assigned to exactly one damage class. It also introduces representative CNN architectures, transfer learning, and data augmentation.

text: 2.2. Convolutional Neural Networks
2.2.1. Overview and Basic Architecture of CNNs

A convolutional neural network (CNN) processes grid-structured data such as images by learning local patterns and combining them across successive layers. Local connectivity restricts each filter to a small region, while parameter sharing applies the same filter at different spatial positions. These properties reduce the number of parameters relative to a fully connected transformation of the same image [1, Ch. 9].
parts: A convolutional neural network (CNN) processes grid-structured data such as images by learning local patterns and combining them across successive layers. Local connectivity restricts each filter to a small region, while parameter sharing applies the same filter at different spatial positions. These properties reduce the number of parameters relative to a fully connected transformation of the same image [1, Ch. 9].

text: A typical CNN classifier consists of convolutional layers, nonlinear activation functions, optional normalization and pooling layers, and a classification head. Earlier layers can represent edges and textures, while later layers combine them into features useful for classification. Convolution provides translation equivariance under appropriate stride and boundary conditions: shifting the input shifts its feature responses. It does not by itself guarantee that the final prediction is invariant to every translation [1, Ch. 9].

text: 2.2.2. Convolutional Layer

An input mini-batch is represented by $X\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times C_{\mathrm{in}}\times H\times W}$, where $B$ is the number of images, $C_{\mathrm{in}}$ is the number of input channels, and $H,W$ are the image height and width. A channel is one two-dimensional component of the tensor. An RGB image has three channels; in a hidden layer, channels contain learned responses rather than raw color values. A feature map is the spatial array of responses associated with one output channel [2, Sec. 7.4].

text: 2.2.3. Activation Functions

Activation functions introduce nonlinearity into the network. Without nonlinear operations, a sequence of affine layers is equivalent to a single affine transformation. Common elementwise activation functions are [1, Sec. 6.3]:
parts: Activation functions introduce nonlinearity into the network. Without nonlinear operations, a sequence of affine layers is equivalent to a single affine transformation. Common elementwise activation functions are [1, Sec. 6.3]:

text: \operatorname{ReLU}(z)=\max(0,z),\qquad \sigma(z)=\frac{1}{1+e^{-z}},\qquad \tanh(z)=\frac{e^z-e^{-z}}{e^z+e^{-z}}

ReLU is inexpensive and has derivative 1 for positive inputs and 0 for negative inputs. It avoids saturation on the positive side, although units that remain inactive can receive zero gradients. Sigmoid maps values to $(0,1)$, and tanh maps them to $(-1,1)$; both can produce small gradients when the magnitude of their input is large. The project uses ReLU in its hidden layers [12].

text: 2.2.4. Pooling Layer

Pooling summarizes a spatial neighborhood within each channel. It usually reduces height and width while preserving the number of channels, lowering the size of subsequent feature tensors. For a pooling region $\mathcal R_{i,j}$, max pooling and average pooling are defined as [1, Sec. 9.3]:
parts: Pooling summarizes a spatial neighborhood within each channel. It usually reduces height and width while preserving the number of channels, lowering the size of subsequent feature tensors. For a pooling region
, max pooling and average pooling are defined as [1, Sec. 9.3]:

text: P^{\mathrm{max}}_{n,c,i,j}=\max_{(u,v)\in\mathcal R_{i,j}}A_{n,c,u,v}
P^{\mathrm{avg}}_{n,c,i,j}=\frac{1}{|\mathcal R_{i,j}|}\sum_{(u,v)\in\mathcal R_{i,j}}A_{n,c,u,v}

Max pooling retains the strongest response in a region, whereas average pooling summarizes all responses in that region. Pooling can reduce sensitivity to small local shifts, but it also discards spatial detail. Global average pooling reduces each entire feature map to one value; adaptive average pooling can instead produce a specified spatial grid [2, Sec. 7.5].

text: 2.2.5. Fully Connected Layer and Softmax

After feature extraction, flattening or pooling converts feature maps into a vector $\mathbf a$. A fully connected layer combines these features through an affine transformation. The final layer produces one logit for each of the $M$ classes [1, Ch. 6]:
parts: After feature extraction, flattening or pooling converts feature maps into a vector
. A fully connected layer combines these features through an affine transformation. The final layer produces one logit for each of the

text: \mathbf z=W_{\mathrm{fc}}\mathbf a+\mathbf b_{\mathrm{fc}},\qquad p_k=\frac{\exp(z_k)}{\sum_{j=1}^{M}\exp(z_j)},\qquad \widehat y=\arg\max_k p_k

Softmax converts logits into probabilities that sum to one. It is appropriate here because the classes are mutually exclusive. The project returns logits directly and passes them to PyTorch CrossEntropyLoss, which incorporates log-softmax internally; an explicit softmax layer is unnecessary during training [12; 13].

text: 2.2.6. Batch Normalization

Batch normalization (BN) normalizes activations separately for each channel. For $X\in\mathbb{R}^{B\times C\times H\times W}$, training statistics are computed over the batch and all spatial positions, not across channels [4, Algorithm 1 and Sec. 3.2]:
parts: Batch normalization (BN) normalizes activations separately for each channel. For
, training statistics are computed over the batch and all spatial positions, not across channels [4, Algorithm 1 and Sec. 3.2]:

text: \mu_c=\frac{1}{BHW}\sum_{n=1}^{B}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\sum_{w=1}^{W}X_{n,c,h,w}
\sigma_c^2=\frac{1}{BHW}\sum_{n=1}^{B}\sum_{h=1}^{H}\sum_{w=1}^{W}(X_{n,c,h,w}-\mu_c)^2
Y_{n,c,h,w}=\gamma_c\frac{X_{n,c,h,w}-\mu_c}{\sqrt{\sigma_c^2+\epsilon}}+\beta_c

Each channel has a learned scale $\gamma_c$ and shift $\beta_c$; $\epsilon>0$ ensures numerical stability. During inference, stored running statistics replace the current batch statistics. The project uses Conv–BN–ReLU blocks. This normalization supports optimization but does not decorrelate channels or perform full whitening [4; 12].

text: 2.3. CNN Training and Optimization
2.3.1. Forward Propagation and Loss Function

Forward propagation transforms an input mini-batch through the network to obtain logits and class probabilities. For $B$ examples and $M$ classes, the mean categorical cross-entropy loss is [1, Sec. 6.2; 13]:
parts: Forward propagation transforms an input mini-batch through the network to obtain logits and class probabilities. For
classes, the mean categorical cross-entropy loss is [1, Sec. 6.2; 13]:

text: \mathcal L_{\mathcal B}(\theta)=-\frac{1}{B}\sum_{n=1}^{B}\sum_{k=1}^{M}y_{n,k}\log p_{n,k}(\theta)

The one-hot target $y_{n,k}$ equals 1 for the correct class and 0 otherwise; $p_{n,k}$ is the predicted probability, and $\theta$ contains the trainable parameters. Thus, each example contributes the negative logarithm of the probability assigned to its correct class. Minimizing this loss encourages larger probabilities for the observed labels. Integer class labels can be used directly in the implementation without explicitly creating one-hot vectors [13].

text: 2.3.2. Backpropagation and Mini-Batch Gradient Descent

Backpropagation applies the chain rule from the loss toward earlier layers. It computes gradients; the optimizer then uses those gradients to update parameters. For the mean softmax cross-entropy loss above, the gradient with respect to each output logit is:

text: \frac{\partial\mathcal L_{\mathcal B}}{\partial z_{n,k}}=\frac{p_{n,k}-y_{n,k}}{B}

To illustrate the backward pass of a convolution, consider the cross-correlation in Section 2.2.2 with unit stride, unit dilation, and no padding. Let $\delta_{n,o,i,j}=\partial\mathcal L_{\mathcal B}/\partial Z_{n,o,i,j}$ be the gradient arriving at its pre-activation output. Applying the chain rule gives:

Adam uses the mini-batch gradient $g_t$ to update each parameter through running moment estimates. All vector products, squares, square roots, and divisions below are elementwise [5].

The first moment $m_t$ smooths the gradient direction; $\beta_1$ controls how much past information is retained.

text: 2.3.4. Overfitting and Regularization

Overfitting occurs when a model fits the training data more closely than is useful for predicting unseen examples. A widening training–validation performance gap can indicate overfitting. Regularization reduces this risk through constraints on learning or additional variability during training [1, Ch. 7].
parts: Overfitting occurs when a model fits the training data more closely than is useful for predicting unseen examples. A widening training–validation performance gap can indicate overfitting. Regularization reduces this risk through constraints on learning or additional variability during training [1, Ch. 7].

text: \mathcal J_{\mathcal B}(\theta)=\mathcal L_{\mathcal B}(\theta)+\frac{\lambda}{2}\|\theta\|_2^2

An L2 penalty discourages large values of the penalized parameters, contributing $\lambda\theta$ to their gradient. The project passes weight_decay to Adam, implementing this coupled penalty in the current training setup; this should not be confused with the decoupled update used by AdamW [12; 14].

text: 2.4.2. Accuracy and Multiclass Precision Recall and F1 Score
Overall accuracy is the fraction of evaluated images classified correctly:
parts: Overall accuracy is the fraction of evaluated images classified correctly:

text: \operatorname{Accuracy}=\frac{\sum_{k=1}^{M}C_{k,k}}{N},\qquad N=\sum_{i=1}^{M}\sum_{j=1}^{M}C_{i,j}
For each class $k$, a one-versus-rest view defines its true positives, false positives, false negatives, and support:
parts: , a one-versus-rest view defines its true positives, false positives, false negatives, and support:

text: \mathrm{TP}_k=C_{k,k},\qquad \mathrm{FP}_k=\sum_{i\ne k}C_{i,k},\qquad \mathrm{FN}_k=\sum_{j\ne k}C_{k,j},\qquad s_k=\sum_j C_{k,j}
P_k=\frac{\mathrm{TP}_k}{\mathrm{TP}_k+\mathrm{FP}_k},\qquad R_k=\frac{\mathrm{TP}_k}{\mathrm{TP}_k+\mathrm{FN}_k},\qquad F_{1,k}=\frac{2\mathrm{TP}_k}{2\mathrm{TP}_k+\mathrm{FP}_k+\mathrm{FN}_k}

Precision measures how often predictions of class $k$ are correct. Recall measures how many actual examples of that class are recovered. F1 combines precision and recall through their harmonic mean. If a denominator is zero, the metric requires an explicit convention; the project assigns zero using zero_division=0 [7; 12].

text: 2.4.3. Training and Validation Loss and Early Stopping

Training loss measures the objective on training examples, while validation loss measures predictive error on held-out examples without updating model parameters. The project records sample-weighted mean cross-entropy for each epoch. Its validation pass uses evaluation mode, so dropout is disabled and BN uses running statistics [12].
parts: Training loss measures the objective on training examples, while validation loss measures predictive error on held-out examples without updating model parameters. The project records sample-weighted mean cross-entropy for each epoch. Its validation pass uses evaluation mode, so dropout is disabled and BN uses running statistics [12].

text: L_{\mathrm{val}}^{(t)}=-\frac{1}{N_{\mathrm{val}}}\sum_{n=1}^{N_{\mathrm{val}}}\log p_{n,y_n}^{(t)}

A persistently decreasing training loss accompanied by a rising validation loss can indicate overfitting. Individual fluctuations are not conclusive, and training loss can exceed validation loss because training uses augmentation and dropout. Early stopping limits unnecessary training by monitoring whether validation loss improves sufficiently [1, Sec. 7.8].

Individual fluctuations are not conclusive, and training loss can exceed validation loss because training uses augmentation and dropout. Early stopping limits unnecessary training by monitoring whether validation loss improves sufficiently [1, Sec. 7.8].

text: 2.5. Representative CNN Architectures
2.5.1. LeNet

LeNet-5 is an early CNN designed for handwritten character recognition. It processes a $32\times32$ grayscale input through convolution, subsampling, and classification stages. Its C1 layer produces six feature maps, S2 reduces their spatial resolution, C3 produces 16 feature maps, and S4 performs further subsampling. C5 combines the remaining spatial features, followed by the F6 layer and the output stage [8].

Its C1 layer produces six feature maps, S2 reduces their spatial resolution, C3 produces 16 feature maps, and S4 performs further subsampling. text: The original architecture uses sigmoid-type nonlinearities and trainable subsampling, with a radial-basis output layer. Modern teaching implementations often replace these details with ReLU, ordinary pooling, and a softmax classifier. LeNet illustrates the central CNN pattern of extracting local features, reducing spatial resolution, and combining the resulting representations for classification [8].

text: VGG uses repeated $3\times3$ convolutions with stride 1 and padding that preserves spatial size within each block. ReLU follows the convolutions, while $2\times2$ max pooling with stride 2 reduces resolution between blocks. The number of feature channels increases as spatial resolution decreases. VGG-16 has 13 convolutional and three fully connected weight layers; VGG-19 has 16 convolutional and three fully connected weight layers [9].

VGG provides a regular architecture that is straightforward to describe and adapt, although its original fully connected classifier accounts for a large share of its parameters and memory requirements [9].

text: 2.5.3. ResNet
ResNet introduces residual blocks to ease the optimization of deep networks. A block learns a residual transformation $F(\mathbf x;W)$ and adds a shortcut from its input [10]:
parts: ResNet introduces residual blocks to ease the optimization of deep networks. A block learns a residual transformation
and adds a shortcut from its input [10]:

text: \mathbf y=F(\mathbf x;W)+\mathbf x
When the spatial dimensions or channel counts differ, a projection $W_s$, commonly implemented by a $1\times1$ convolution with a suitable stride, matches the shortcut to the residual output:
parts: When the spatial dimensions or channel counts differ, a projection
convolution with a suitable stride, matches the shortcut to the residual output:

text: \mathbf y=F(\mathbf x;W)+W_s\mathbf x

The addition provides a direct path for information and gradients, allowing the block to learn a change to its input representation. ResNet-18 and ResNet-34 use basic blocks with two $3\times3$ convolutions; deeper variants such as ResNet-50 use bottleneck blocks with $1\times1$, $3\times3$, and $1\times1$ convolutions. The original networks finish with global average pooling and a fully connected classifier [10].

text: 2.6. Techniques for Improving CNN Performance
2.6.1. Transfer Learning

Transfer learning builds a classifier from a CNN pretrained on a source dataset, such as ImageNet. The pretrained feature extractor is retained, and its original classification layer is replaced by a new head with one output per target class. For this four-class task, the new head therefore has four logits [11].

The pretrained feature extractor is retained, and its original classification layer is replaced by a new head with one output per target class. For this four-class task, the new head therefore has four logits [11].

text: In a feature-extraction setup, the backbone weights are frozen and only the new head is trained. For fine-tuning, selected backbone layers or the full backbone are unfrozen and updated, usually with a smaller learning rate than the newly initialized head. Input preprocessing must match the pretrained weights, and the amount of fine-tuning is selected using validation performance. If the backbone is intended to remain fixed, its BN running statistics must also remain fixed [4; 11].

text: 2.6.2. Data Augmentation

Data augmentation generates varied training inputs through transformations intended to preserve class identity. Random flips, modest geometric changes, and photometric changes expose the model to variations that may occur in unseen images. Transformations must remain appropriate to the task; for example, large rotations can change the directional meaning of a road crack [1, Sec. 7.4].

text: The project applies online horizontal flipping, small affine transformations, color jitter, occasional perspective distortion, and Gaussian blur before tensor conversion and normalization. Augmentation is restricted to training images. Validation and test images receive only tensor conversion and normalization, using statistics computed from the training set. This preserves a consistent evaluation procedure and avoids using validation or test statistics to prepare the training inputs [12].
